How to use this library

One library, every tool

Every tool draws its turns and landing pages from here. Each template carries a badge:

  • Universal pattern: any tool and any place may use it, redrawn in that tool’s own colours by its own generator.
  • [Place] only or [Tool] only: only that place or tool uses it.
  • Approved, variation (a sample not chosen, ready as a pattern) or draft.

Which block, when

  1. Decide the turn type (question, asking for figures, figures back, findings, diagnosis, overview, part, going deeper, challenge, recommendation).
  2. Pick the fewest blocks that carry what the chat cannot: approved first, then variations. Each block below says use when and avoid when.
  3. Never reuse a place’s main block in the next turn: every turn looks different. A fill-in-the-blank and its answered redraw are the one exception.
  4. Mark each figure as yours, worked out from yours, a guess, an example, a goal, or needed.

How a turn is built

Claude writes one JSON spec: the user’s message, the chat parts (text, note, @points, one question, three prompts) and the blocks with their words. The tool’s generator checks it and draws it. Nobody writes HTML by hand. Rules: rules/06 (response), rules/07 (block design), rules/08 (shared turn rules).

Chat panel (written by Claude)
Discharge delays. Our patients are medically fit by mid-morning but most don’t leave till late afternoon.

Before I suggest anything, I want to see how discharge really runs in your hospital. Most delays that look like discharge problems start further up the chain.

First stop, the doctors: who writes the discharge summary, who reviews it, who signs it — and when do rounds finish on your busiest wards?

The whole route is laid out for you — tap any stop to see what I’ll ask there.

Tojo’s note

Most delays start long before the billing desk.

Chat panel (written by Claude)
@Point1 @Point2One bed earns about ₹32,000 a day. Most patients are ready by 10 and leave around 3, so they wait about 5 hours. The doctors usually decide who’s going home on the 7 PM round, but they don’t sign till morning.

Your real problem isn’t slow discharge. It’s time nobody uses, and nobody being in charge.

Here’s why. Your doctors already decide in the evening. But nothing happens until they sign the next morning. Most of the going-home work could be done overnight. Nobody does it today because:

  • Nothing is automatic, so starting early means doing the work twice.
  • No team moves until the doctor signs.
  • Nobody has ever been asked to use the evening.

The second reason: your own numbers show you now need one person in charge of discharge. Does this match what you see on the wards?

Chat panel (written by Claude)
Yes, that’s exactly it. Show me how to fix it.

Here’s what the fix is made of. It has five parts.

None of them needs a new hospital system on day one. They sit on top of how you work today.

Each part opens to show what’s in it. Pick the one you want to start with.

Tojo’s note

Five parts, one aim: put the evening to work.

Add to a point — pick one or more
Or ask next
Mobile canvas · 362px
The fix

What the fix is made of

Five parts. Open any one to see what’s in it.

Automatic paperworkStart here

What the software does, so nobody does the work twice.

See what it doesClose

Other hospitals saved 6 to 8 hours for each patient. Not yet measured here.

  • Starts the going-home papers when a doctor first mentions it, even on the evening round.
  • Keeps a record of every test, medicine and procedure from the day the patient arrives.
  • Keeps the bill up to date all the time, so it is ready the moment the doctor signs.
  • Works out which unused medicines go back to pharmacy, so nurses don’t count them first.
  • Sends a first bill to the insurance company the evening before.
  • Lets the doctor check and sign on a phone or tablet during the morning round.
Changes on the wardsPart 2

What each team does differently, step by step.

See the changesClose
  • The steps stay the same. They start earlier and run side by side.
  • Staff approve what the software prepares, instead of writing it by hand.
  • Your IT team connects the software to your hospital systems, reports and notes.
  • Pharmacy, diet, housekeeping and transport teams are told exactly when they’re needed.
  • If one team does both discharges and admissions, the two jobs are split or run together.
  • The bed desk writes down when each bed is given out and when the next patient arrives.
People who must agreePart 3

Who has to say yes, and what each is asked to do.

See who and whyClose

Each team is told the software takes work off them. It does not replace them.

  • Doctors: start the going-home papers in the evening, then sign on a phone next morning.
  • Nurses: check what the software writes down from the doctors’ notes.
  • Billing and the insurance desk: check bills that are already made.
  • IT, lab and scan teams: keep reports up to date in the system.
  • Admissions, housekeeping, the dietitian and the ward manager: act when the software tells them.
  • Head of Operations: approves the new order of steps. Without this, the change won’t last.
Who is in chargePart 4

Whether you need someone new to run this.

See the rolesClose
  • Most teams only record and approve a little more in the system.
  • A Discharge Manager runs the whole process and works with the other departments. About ₹4 to 4.5 lakh a year.
  • Discharge Executives look after each patient going home. About ₹3 to 3.5 lakh a year each.
  • How many executives you need depends on your busiest hours. We work that out together.
How we’ll know it workedPart 5

The few numbers we will watch, week by week.

See what we’ll trackClose
  • Time from the doctor saying ‘go home’ to the patient leaving.
  • How many patients paying themselves leave by 10 AM (11 AM at the latest), and insured patients by 1 PM.
  • How many going-home decisions start on the evening round.
  • How long insurance approval takes, in the evening and in the morning.
  • How long a bed takes to be ready for the next patient.
  • Whether every family hears about diet, medicines and follow-up before leaving.

What it asks of your staffStaff

To check and approve, instead of writing everything by hand.

  • Billing and the insurance desk: check bills that are already made.
  • At first it only helps each person. It takes work away only once everyone trusts it.
What must happen firstNeeded first

Your IT team links the software to your hospital systems.

See why this mattersClose
  • The software can only record what it can read, so it needs your patient records, bills, lab reports and scans.
  • Without this link, nothing above works. It is the first job, before anything else.
  • Lab and scan teams need to put reports in on time, so the records stay complete.

Start with the automatic paperwork

Here’s what the software does in your hospital, from the 7 PM round to the patient going home. Why each piece matters:

  • It starts at the evening round, because your doctors already decide then. Nothing new is asked of them.
  • It keeps the bill up to date all day, so billing stops waiting for the nurses to count supplies.
  • It sends the first bill to insurance overnight, so the morning isn’t spent waiting for approval.

One team for leaving and arrivingCheck this

The two jobs queue behind each other every morning.

Two ways to fix itClose
  • Split the work into two teams, one for patients leaving and one for patients arriving.
  • Or run both at the same time, so admissions don’t wait for discharges to finish.
  • Either way it costs nothing but agreeing the new order. The Head of Operations signs it off.
What other teams watch forOther teams

The software tells each team when it is their turn.

See which teamsClose
  • The bed desk: when a bed will be free, and when the next patient arrives.
  • Pharmacy: which medicines are coming back.
  • The dietitian: which families need a diet talk before leaving.
  • Housekeeping and transport: when to clean the bed and bring the wheelchair.

Show me the changes on the wards

Most of the work stays the same. What changes is when it starts, and who writes it. Why these changes:

  • Starting in the evening only works if each team knows it has started, so the software tells them.
  • Staff approve instead of writing, so nobody does the same work twice.
  • The discharge papers are the biggest hold-up today, so they change the most.

Chat panel (written by Claude)
Show me who is in charge

You need one person to own discharge, and two people to run it day to day. Why:

  • Nobody owns the whole wait today, and your own numbers are past the lines where one owner is needed.
  • Two helpers, not three, because your work comes in two busy times of day, not spread across 24 hours.
  • Every other team only records and approves a little more. Their jobs don’t change.

Last part: how we’ll know it worked. Shall we go there?

Discharge ManagerOwner

Owns the whole process, from the evening decision to the empty bed.

See the roleClose
  • One person answers for every delay, instead of each team blaming the process.

  • About ₹4 to 4.5 lakh a year.
Discharge ExecutivesDaily

Look after each patient going home, and chase every delay.

See the roleClose
  • Take over each patient from the moment the doctor decides on the evening round.
  • Spot delays as they happen, and chase the team holding things up.
  • About ₹3 to 3.5 lakh a year each.

Chat panel (written by Claude)
Show me how we’ll know it worked

We’ll watch a short list of numbers, week by week. Where you already gave me a number, that is where we start. Why these:

  • They measure the wait itself, not how busy people are, so a busy week can’t hide a slow one.
  • They start from your own numbers, so progress is measured against you, not against other hospitals.
  • Nothing tracks some of them today. Those are marked new, and the first week of the trial gives their starting number.

That’s all five parts. Shall I put them into a plan, starting with a short trial?

Mobile canvas · 362px
Part 5 of 5 · Knowing it worked

The numbers we will watch

Hours from ready to homeYours

Starting number: 5 hours, from you.

How we measure itClose
  • From the doctor saying the patient can go, to the patient leaving the building.
  • Counted for every patient, not a sample.
  • Reported every week, ward by ward.
Home by 10 AMGoal

Goal: patients paying themselves home by 10 AM, 11 at the latest. Insured patients by 1 PM.

How we measure itClose
  • The share of each day’s patients who have left by those times.
  • No starting number yet. The first week of the trial sets it.
Decided on the evening roundNew

The share of going-home decisions made at 7 PM.

Why it mattersClose
  • It shows whether the evening is really being used. That is the heart of the fix.
  • The software records it by itself, so nobody fills in a form.
Insurance approval timeNew

How long the insurer takes, in the evening and in the morning.

Why it mattersClose
  • It shows whether sending the first bill overnight is working.
  • The insurer is outside your control, so this is kept apart from your own delays.
Bed ready for the next patientNew

Time from the patient leaving to the bed being ready again.

How we measure itClose
  • Includes the wait before housekeeping is told, not only the cleaning.
  • Checked against the bed desk’s own times.
Money won backYours

Freed beds given to new patients, against the ₹10.3 crore a year at stake.

How we measure itClose
  • Only beds that are really filled again count, not beds that are just freed.
  • The new roles pay for themselves at about 1% of this.

Week 1: watchWeek 1

Run discharge the usual way, and write down every time above.

Week 2: the new orderWeek 2

Start the papers, the bill and insurance on the evening round, by hand.

See what changesClose
  • Doctors say who is going home on the evening round, as they already do.

  • The same times are written down, so the two weeks can be compared.

Compare the two weeks, and decide what to link first.

Desktop canvas · 864px
Automatic paperworkStart here

What the software does, so nobody does the work twice.

See what it doesClose

Other hospitals saved 6 to 8 hours for each patient. Not yet measured here.

  • Starts the going-home papers when a doctor first mentions it, even on the evening round.
  • Keeps a record of every test, medicine and procedure from the day the patient arrives.
  • Keeps the bill up to date all the time, so it is ready the moment the doctor signs.
  • Works out which unused medicines go back to pharmacy, so nurses don’t count them first.
  • Sends a first bill to the insurance company the evening before.
  • Lets the doctor check and sign on a phone or tablet during the morning round.
Changes on the wardsPart 2

What each team does differently, step by step.

See the changesClose
  • The steps stay the same. They start earlier and run side by side.
  • Staff approve what the software prepares, instead of writing it by hand.
  • Your IT team connects the software to your hospital systems, reports and notes.
  • Pharmacy, diet, housekeeping and transport teams are told exactly when they’re needed.
  • If one team does both discharges and admissions, the two jobs are split or run together.
  • The bed desk writes down when each bed is given out and when the next patient arrives.
People who must agreePart 3

Who has to say yes, and what each is asked to do.

See who and whyClose

Each team is told the software takes work off them. It does not replace them.

  • Doctors: start the going-home papers in the evening, then sign on a phone next morning.
  • Nurses: check what the software writes down from the doctors’ notes.
  • Billing and the insurance desk: check bills that are already made.
  • IT, lab and scan teams: keep reports up to date in the system.
  • Admissions, housekeeping, the dietitian and the ward manager: act when the software tells them.
  • Head of Operations: approves the new order of steps. Without this, the change won’t last.

The trial is planned. Nothing has changed on the wards yet.

Changes, measures and new roles in one place. A two-week trial on one ward comes first.

Process changes

5 agreed on paper · 1 new · 0 tried
  • The evening round starts the paperwork
  • Discharge papers drafted before signingBiggest hold-up
  • Bill and supply count kept up to date
  • Insurance asked the evening before
  • Family and transport told the night before
  • Bed made ready as the patient leaves

Measures we watch

3 with a starting number · 3 new
  • Hours from ready to home5 hours 15 minutes
  • Insurance approval timeAbout 1 hour
  • Bed empty after the patient leaves75 minutes
  • Patients home by 10 AMNew
  • Decisions made on the evening roundNew
  • Money won back each monthNew

Team and role changes

3 people to hire · ₹10 to 11.5 lakh a year
  • Discharge ManagerRecommended now, before the trial
  • Discharge ExecutivesOne for 8 to 11 AM, one for 6 to 9 PM
  • ₹10 to 11.5 lakh a year. Your Head of Operations approves.

Desktop canvas · 864px
Findings
  1. What you told us

    Patients are ready by 10 in the morning but leave at about 3:15 in the afternoon.

  2. What is really happening

    Doctors decide in the evening, but nothing starts until they sign the next morning.

  3. Why

    The overnight hours go unused, and no one person owns the whole discharge.

Discharge Process

The first tool, regenerated on 5 Oct 2026 with the latest generators: the ones built for Bed Management, loaded as copies and pointed at Discharge. Every turn has its own drawing, plain simple English, the common tool layer (the first item raised with its sheet open; on a phone every item stacked with its sheet under it; entries typed in the drawing and added to the message), the three buttons, and a background that changes every four turns. Same practice hospital as before: 250 beds, Bhubaneswar. Each place keeps the colours of its approved landing page.

Diagnosis turn templates

3 turns in conversation order, drawn by Discharge Process/diagnosis-html-generator/dp_diagnosis_html.py in the Discharge Diagnosis look: the case sheet: sage ground, forest ink. Every turn ends with Proceed with next step, Add more, Jump to Solutions. Each note says which old template it replaces.

dp-dg-01 · The road to going home turn
approvedDischarge Process only

dp-dg-01 · The road to going home. Was turn-01. The eleven stops as rooms on one path: the agenda, walked one stop at a time.

User’s message: Discharge delays. Our patients are medically fit by mid-morning but most don’t leave till late afternoon.
Blocks: ward-map · Theme: The case sheet (base) · Replaces: turn-01 (dp-01), route-map · Review: Approved 6 Oct with the regenerated Discharge turns.

Desktop canvas · 864px
The road home · stop 1 of 11

The road to going home

Eleven stops, each run by a different team. We walk them one at a time.

Doctor decides11 stops, one team eachBed ready
  1. Stop 1 of 11

    The doctors

    The summary is drafted, checked and signed by different people. The round decides when any of it can start.

    What we often hearDischarges are just slow
    Who writes, checks and signs the summary?
    In your message
  2. Stop 2 of 11

    Supply count

    The bill cannot be finished until nurses count the used supplies. They count only when they are free.

    What we often hearBilling is slow
    How long after signing do nurses start counting?
    In your message
  3. Stop 3 of 11

    Pharmacy returns

    What was given, what was used and what goes back. Counted by hand, it means a second pass on the bill.

    What we often hearStill waiting on pharmacy
    Who works out the medicines going back?
    In your message
  4. Stop 4 of 11

    Billing

    A charge that arrives after the bill is closed opens it again.

    What we often hearBills changed at the counter
    How many bills were reopened last month?
    In your message
  5. Stop 5 of 11

    Insurance desk

    The insurer’s approval sits inside the family’s wait.

    Does your discharge time include the insurance wait?
    In your message
  6. Stop 6 of 11

    Bed desk

    Discharge times can only be checked against when beds were given out.

    Can the bed desk say when beds were given?
    In your message
  7. Stop 7 of 11

    Housekeeping

    A bed is cleaned from when housekeeping hears, not from when the patient left.

    How long until housekeeping hears a bed is free?
    In your message
  8. Stop 8 of 11

    Transport

    Porters are shared with admissions and scans, at the same busy hour.

    How many porters work at the busy hour?
    In your message
  9. Stop 9 of 11

    Operating theatre

    A bed freed late cannot be used for an operation that same day.

    What is the latest a freed bed helps?
    In your message
  10. Stop 10 of 11

    Last checks

    The dietitian, the pharmacist and the nurse must each see the patient, in no set order.

    Who must see the patient before they leave?
    In your message
  11. Stop 11 of 11

    Cash counter

    Every patient going home meets one counter, in the same two hours.

    Who can let a patient go with money owed?
    In your message

Automations · on the round

Three steps, one yes each

What happens between the doctor’s word and the draft on their phone.

AutomationsThe evening round
  1. Idea
  2. Built
  3. Testing
  4. Switched on

Pick a step. The loop lights where Tojo is, and its sheet opens.

Tojo’s loop: it notices, gathers, checks, drafts, then asks a person.
On the evening round
  2. On the evening round

    Hear the decision

    The doctor taps once on the ward phone to say the patient can likely go tomorrow. Tojo takes that as its signal.

    A person’s hand here: the doctorTaps once to say the patient can likely go.
    Checks first
    It is the patient’s own doctor
    And
    The patient is not waiting on a test
    What would stop a patient going tomorrow?
    In your message
  4. Within minutes

    Put the draft together

    Tojo gathers the facts recorded since admission. It writes the draft summary, the expected bill and the medicines to take home.

    Checks first
    Every test result is in
    And
    The bill matches what was used
    Which part of the summary is hardest to write?
    In your message
  6. Before the round ends

    Ask for the yes

    The draft is on the doctor’s phone. Anything missing or unclear is marked for the doctor to look at.

    A person’s hand here: the doctorReads the early summary, then signs or corrects it.
    Checks first
    Late reports are named, never guessed
    Who else should see the draft?
    In your message

Desktop canvas · 864px
Automations · your IT team

Five asks, nothing changed

Each ask only reads, or is a one-off. Your IT team changes nothing in your systems.

AutomationsThe IT links
  1. Idea
  2. Built
  3. Testing
  4. Switched on

Pick an ask to see why it is needed and who in IT does it.

One question for you first. Then these five things for your IT team. None of it is needed today.
What I would ask IT
  2. Ask 1 of 5

    Read-only access to billing and notes

    Tojo only reads. Nothing can be changed or deleted.

    Who does it
    Your IT team, once
    Who could give read-only access?
    In your message
  4. Ask 2 of 5

    Each report, as it is signed

    So the summary never waits for a report.

    Who does it
    Your IT team, with the lab
    How do reports reach doctors today?
    In your message
  6. Ask 3 of 5

    The list of charges and their prices

    So the bill can be kept up to date, charge by charge.

    Who does it
    Billing, with IT
    Where is your price list kept?
    In your message
  8. Ask 4 of 5

    A test copy of one ward’s records

    With the patient names hidden. So we can try it before any real patient.

    Who does it
    Your IT team, once
    Which ward could we copy?
    In your message
  10. Ask 5 of 5

    One named person in your IT team

    One contact, so questions do not wait.

    Who does it
    Your Head of IT
    Who looks after your hospital software?
    In your message

  2. New role

    Two, one for each busy time

    Which consultants decide latest?

    Papers take 1½ hours

    This is the typing step the software removes. It was the biggest hold-up I expected, and your times agree.

    Held up
    The biggest hold-up
  3. New

    Bed ready 75 minutes later

    Part of this may be waiting for housekeeping to hear. We will check it in the trial.

    Under 30 minutes
    How does housekeeping hear today?

Desktop canvas · 864px
Processes · who agrees

Nine badges, one approver

Each badge says where that person stands. Most are still to ask.

Ward boardWho agrees
  1. Changes
  2. People
  3. Roles
  4. Measures
  5. The trial

Pick a name badge to see what changes for that person.

Approves the flow

  • Approves the flow

    Head of Operations

    Signs off the new order of work across departments. Takes no part in the daily tasks.

    What they gain
    One Discharge Manager reports the numbers every week.
    What would your Head of Operations say?
    In your message

Works on the trial ward

  • Works on the trial ward

    Doctors

    Mark likely discharges on the evening round with one tap. Sign the early summary.

    What they gain
    The summary is ready to check, not to write.
    What you told us
    “Our doctors don’t use voice notes.” So the trial uses a tap.
    What would doctors say?
    In your message
  • Works on the trial ward

    Nurses

    Record the ready and leaving times. Start the papers after the evening round.

    What they gain
    No rush for medicines and papers at noon.
    What would nurses say?
    In your message
  • Works on the trial ward

    Billing

    Checks a bill kept up to date all stay, instead of building it at the end.

    What they gain
    No pile of bills at noon.
    What would billing say?
    In your message
  • Works on the trial ward

    Insurance desk

    Sends the early request the evening before.

    What they gain
    Fewer calls chasing the insurer the next day.
    What would insurance desk say?
    In your message

Watches for updates

  • Watches for updates

    Housekeeping

    Hears the moment a patient leaves, with the bed number.

    What they gain
    No waiting for a phone call.
    What would housekeeping say?
    In your message
  • Watches for updates

    Pharmacy and diet

    Told that evening who goes home tomorrow.

    What they gain
    Medicines packed before the morning rush.
    What would pharmacy and diet say?
    In your message
  • Watches for updates

    Bed desk

    Sees each bed turn ready without a call.

    What they gain
    The next patient is placed sooner.
    What would bed desk say?
    In your message

After the trial

  • After the trial

    IT team

    Lets Tojo read the hospital software. Nothing can be changed or deleted.

    What they gain
    One clear list, asked for once.
    What would your IT team say?
    In your message

Tojo comes in as help with each job, not a threat to it. Any fall in staff hours comes later, once it is trusted.

Discharge Processes drawings

Drawn for Discharge where the latest generators had no drawing that fits; the rest of the place uses the layered library drawings shown in the turns above.

heading Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: library heading (Processes), with the ward board from the Processes landing page. Eyebrow, title and deck, with a small ward board: which column of the board this turn is about.

Use when: every turn
Avoid when: never twice
Drawn in: dp-pr-01, shown above

swap Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Each step of the day, its magnet moved from today to with the changes.

Use when: what changes on the ward, step by step
Avoid when: fewer than three steps
Interaction: Pick a step to open it. Move one magnet, or all of them with the switch.
Drawn in: dp-pr-10, shown above

trial Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The two weeks on one ward: the day strip you can play, the phases as pickable bands, the ward still to choose.

Use when: scoping a short trial
Avoid when: no trial
Interaction: Pick a phase, or play the two weeks. Type the ward you choose.
Drawn in: dp-pr-08, shown above

badges Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Name badges on the board, grouped by what each person does: who agrees, who is still to ask, who has a worry.

Use when: who has to agree, team by team
Avoid when: one approver only
Interaction: Pick a badge to open it. Filter by the trial or still to ask.
Drawn in: dp-pr-09, shown above

seats Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The roles as chairs, their triggers as lamps, the busy-hours check as a day strip with a slider.

Use when: whether to hire, and how many
Avoid when: no new roles
Interaction: Pick a role to open it. Move the slider and switch the sizing rule.
Drawn in: dp-pr-11, shown above

readouts Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The measures as instrument windows: the starting number where there is one, dashed where nobody has one yet.

Use when: the measures to watch
Avoid when: fewer than three measures
Interaction: Pick a window to open it. Filter by when it is read; flip to after the trial.
Drawn in: dp-pr-13, shown above

loop Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Plan, try, measure, adjust, spread: a wheel with a yes-or-no check that sends you on or back.

Use when: what happens after a trial
Avoid when: a one-off step
Interaction: Step round, or pick a step. At the check, answer yes or not yet.
Drawn in: dp-pr-14, shown above

timesheet Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. One normal day’s times on one line. Blank: the times are typed straight into the drawing. Filled: the times and the gaps between them.

Use when: asking for real times; showing them back
Avoid when: no times
Interaction: Type a time on each step (blank), or pick a step to open it (filled).
Drawn in: dp-pr-06, shown above

night-lanes Discharge Processes drawing
approvedDischarge Process only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Each job on one clock from the evening round to the next afternoon: when it happens today, and with the changes.

Use when: the same work started the night before
Avoid when: daytime only
Interaction: Pick a job to open it. Switch between today and with the changes.
Drawn in: dp-pr-01, shown above

Bed Management

The second tool. Same layout as every tool, its own colours and drawings. Each place has its own palette; the home page is a ward plan, and every place page draws from it. Turn templates use the universal patterns above, redrawn in Bed Management’s colours, with the common tool layer on top.

Bed Management · the look palette
approvedBed Management only

One palette per place. Gold #d4a94f is now, next and picked in every place; the chat panel stays forest. Turn backgrounds change every four turns (Diagnosis: the morning count, then the lamp-lit sheet. Solutions: the fit-out, then plan paper).

The changes

One named person on each shift keeps the bed list right and chases every empty bed.

How it will work
  • Named at the start of each shift, on the board
  • Checks the bed list every two hours
  • Calls housekeeping for each empty bed

Patients who can go home leave before 11 AM, so their beds are ready for the morning’s new patients.

How it will work
  • Doctors mark tomorrow’s discharges on the evening round
  • Papers and medicines ready the night before
  • The family told the evening before

  • At the nurses’ station, standing, ten minutes
  • The ward, housekeeping and admissions all there
  • Agrees the day’s free beds and when each will be ready

bm-dg-03 · Which day is closer to yours? turn
approvedBed Management only

bm-dg-03 · Which day is closer to yours?.

Turn: Transcript turn 9 · the follow-up to “one team” · Blocks: day-strips · Review: Approved by Avishek with the second Diagnosis set (one drawing per turn).

Desktop canvas · 864px
One team, two ways to run the day

Which day is closer to yours?

The same three moments of the day, run two ways. Read across each row.

8 AM10 AMNoon2 PM4 PM6 PM
Pattern A

Discharges first, admissions later

The team finishes one job before it starts the other. New patients wait for the switch.

MorningDischarges first, through the morning
MiddayThe team switches to admissions
Afternoon and eveningAdmissions land late in the day
Pattern B

Both jobs side by side

The team works both jobs together. New patients are called in before their bed is free.

MorningDischarges and admissions worked together
MiddayPatients already called in for beds due to free
Afternoon and eveningAdmissions land across the day
Patients leavingPatients arrivingBoth at onceQuiet

Tap a pattern to read it, moment by moment.

Discharges first, admissions later

The team finishes one job before it starts the other. New patients wait for the switch.

MorningDischarges first, through the morning

Both jobs side by side

The team works both jobs together. New patients are called in before their bed is free.

Afternoon and eveningAdmissions land across the day

Two neutral patterns, so you can place your own day. Neither one is the answer I expect.

Desktop canvas · 864px
Why it happens

One rule, and the loop it starts

Your five findings come back to one rule. Follow it round once and it starts itself again.

Your five findings lead back to one rule
One team does both jobsAdmission time about 3½ hoursNo set way to match bedsBeds idle 4 to 5 hoursNo team ever sized
The ruleA bed is given only once it is confirmed ready, or about to be.Your own words, with your times
↓
Then 1 of 4

Bed given only when nearly free

No bed is put against a patient ahead of time, even when you know it will free up.

↓
Then 2 of 4

Nobody called in early

Without a bed to give, there is nothing to call a patient in against. Calls wait until late.

↓
Then 3 of 4

Patients arrive and wait

Your own times. Patients arrive in the early afternoon and wait for the bed to catch up.

Then 4 of 4

Beds never seem ready sooner

Because no bed is given early, nobody plans for one to free early. So they don’t, and the rule looks right.

↻And the next morning, the same rule starts the loop again.

Bed Management drawings and the tool layer

The drawings Bed Management Diagnosis uses, one per turn, so no two turns look alike. Each is drawn by Bed Management/diagnosis-html-generator/bm_blocks.py. On a phone every pickable item is stacked, one above the other, and its sheet opens under it.

effect Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Numbers. The quantity a turn names: a label, the figure and one line, in the effect-box fill (07 §5.2) with a small bed-and-bill mark.

Use when: naming the quantity a turn arrives at
Avoid when: more than two in a turn
Drawn in: bm-dg-01, shown above

lens Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. Areas to examine on the rim of a magnifying glass. The one asked now is ink on the rim, the picked one gold.

Use when: showing the areas of enquiry before asking the first
Avoid when: a sequence of steps
Interaction: Pick an area: its arc turns gold and its sheet opens.
Drawn in: bm-dg-02, shown above

day-strips Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. Two ways a day can run, drawn bed by bed, hour by hour: beds with patients leaving, arriving, both, or quiet.

Use when: testing a claim about how a day runs, without leading
Avoid when: one pattern only
Interaction: Pick a pattern to read it.
Drawn in: bm-dg-03, shown above

admission-route Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The patient’s way from the door to the bed, one stop per step, with a clock time at each. Blank: the times are typed in. Filled: the times and the gaps between them.

Use when: asking for, then showing, the steps of an admission with times
Avoid when: billing times
Interaction: Pick a step; in blank mode type its time in the sheet and it appears on the stop.
Drawn in: bm-dg-04, shown above

stopwatch Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. Where the hours of one admission go, on a stopwatch dial: work in ink, waiting hatched amber.

Use when: after the times are in, to show how little of the time is work
Avoid when: before the times are in
Interaction: None: a reading.
Drawn in: bm-dg-05, shown above

bed-bills Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The leaving patient’s bill and the next patient’s first charge, as two tags tied to one bed, with the stretch between them where nothing bills.

Use when: asking for, then showing, the two billing times
Avoid when: admission steps
Interaction: Pick a tag; in blank mode type the time in its sheet.
Drawn in: bm-dg-06, shown above

receipt Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The figures Tojo needs, as lines on a paper bill. Each line takes the figure right there; the total says how many are in.

Use when: a batched ask for figures
Avoid when: figures already given
Interaction: Type each figure on its line; pick a line to see what it turns into.
Drawn in: bm-dg-08, shown above

bed-count Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The beds that change patient each day, drawn one by one, and what the hours won back are worth. A slider sets the hours won back.

Use when: turning a duration into money from the user’s figures
Avoid when: fact-collecting turns
Interaction: Move the slider; pick a figure to see the working.
Drawn in: bm-dg-09, shown above

evidence-board Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The findings pinned to a board in the order they were given, on one thread, each with the user’s own words.

Use when: consolidation before the diagnosis
Avoid when: causal order (that is the diagnosis)
Interaction: Pick a card to see where it came from.
Drawn in: bm-dg-10, shown above

rule-loop Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The diagnosis: the findings feed one rule; the rule starts a loop of consequences that comes back round to it.

Use when: the diagnosis turn
Avoid when: before the evidence is in
Interaction: Pick a step to follow the loop.
Drawn in: bm-dg-11, shown above

scale Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. Demand against supply on a balance, tipping to the heavier side, with the verdict beside it.

Use when: the scaling pivot: whether the full design applies
Avoid when: anything but two quantities
Interaction: None: a reading.
Drawn in: bm-dg-12, shown above

corridor Bed Management drawing
approvedBed Management only only

Drawing. The parts of the answer as closed doors along a corridor. Picking one opens it a little and shows what is behind it, briefly.

Use when: naming the parts of the solution before any is opened
Avoid when: going into one part (that is the next place)
Interaction: Pick a door to look in.
Drawn in: bm-dg-12, shown above

tool layer picking and entries
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

Common. Any generator can add it to time-window, chain, two-flow, cards, stat-strip, converge. Each item of the drawing gets a sheet; the first is raised with its sheet open; on a phone the sheet opens under its item. A sheet may carry an Add yours field: the entry is written into the chat message with where it came from, and every entry is added, never replaced. Code: Common Elements/tool-layer/tojo_layer.py.

Slots it adds: sheets (one per item, in order: key, when, title, text, and each tool’s own lines), ask_more (one closing entry).

Solutions turn templates

Each is drawn by Bed Management/solutions-html-generator/bm_solutions_html.py from its spec, using the Solutions motifs of this library (the lightbulb, the jigsaw, the maze, the knots, the route, the drafting sheet and the door plates) in Bed Management’s Solutions colours, with the common tool layer. Every turn ends with the three buttons: Proceed with next step, Add more, Jump to Automations.

bm-so-01 · Sample A · Six switches, one bulb turn
approvedBed Management only

bm-so-01 · Six switches, one bulb. The lightbulb motif. The six steps are switches on one wire, wrapped three and three with an elbow as the transcript asks. Pick a switch: the current runs from OPD to it, and the bulb lights only at the last one.

Turn: Transcript turn 18 · Part 1: Automation · Blocks: circuit, effect · Theme: The fit-out (base) · Review: Approved 1 Oct: the turn (Avishek’s preference).

Desktop canvas · 864px
Part 1 · Automations

Six switches, one bulb

The automation part, from the OPD to the call-in time. The bed is ready on time only when every switch is on.

Part 1 of 5Automations
  1. Idea
  2. Shaped
  3. Tested with you
  4. Agreed

Pick a switch. The current runs to it, and the bulb lights at the last one.

  1. OPDWhere the advice to admit is written
  3. In OPD, all day

    Admission advice recorded

    Each time an OPD doctor advises admission, the advice is recorded with the procedure and the date. Tomorrow’s planned admissions are known when they are advised, not when the patient turns up.

    Reads from
    The OPD prescription, as the doctor writes it
    Who does the work
    Nobody new. The advice is read, not typed again
    How does admission advice reach your desk today?
    In your message
  5. 2 PM

    First mapping of tomorrow

    Patients arrive about 1 PM, in a bed about 4:30 PM
    With this step
    Each patient is called for their own bed’s time
    Who calls patients in at your hospital today?
    In your message
In OPD, all day

Admission advice recorded

Each time an OPD doctor advises admission, the advice is recorded with the procedure and the date. Tomorrow’s planned admissions are known when they are advised, not when the patient turns up.

Reads from
The OPD prescription, as the doctor writes it
Who does the work
Nobody new. The advice is read, not typed again
How does admission advice reach your desk today?
In your message
2 PM

First mapping of tomorrow

At 2 PM the first pass sets tomorrow’s planned admissions against the beds. It counts empty beds, and beds likely to free up. Those are patients near the usual stay for their own procedure.

Reads from
Admissions, discharges and each patient’s procedure
Gives
A first picture of tomorrow’s beds, ward by ward
Which wards are hardest to predict?
In your message
After 2 PM

Teams told

The wards, housekeeping and the admissions desk are told which beds should free up tomorrow. Each team sees the same list, so nobody works from an old one.

Who sees it
Ward nurses, housekeeping and the admissions desk
Kept up to date
At each pass, 2 PM and 6 PM
Who should hear first at your hospital?
In your message
5 PM

Evening round confirms

On the 5 PM round, the treating doctor confirms which patients will go home tomorrow. This is what makes the 6 PM freeze worth anything. A forecast no doctor has checked is only a guess.

Who
The treating doctor, on the evening round
What changes
The forecast becomes a decision
Do your doctors round in the evening? At what time?
In your message
6 PM

Tomorrow’s plan frozen

At 6 PM tomorrow’s plan is frozen. Each patient coming in is matched to one bed, with the time it should be ready. A late change is handled on its own, not by redoing the plan.

Gives
One plan for every bed tomorrow
Fixed at
6 PM, the evening before
What usually changes the plan after 6 PM?
In your message
After 6 PM

Call-in times sent

The desk is told when to call each patient in, bed by bed. It stops guessing, so patients come when their bed is ready. This step is aimed at your 1 PM arrivals.

Today
Patients arrive about 1 PM, in a bed about 4:30 PM
With this step
Each patient is called for their own bed’s time

Under 30 minutes

bm-so-05 · Run the two jobs together. The approved shape: one big change, four small ones, two owners, then the ask. The decoupling is the hospital’s own answer from Diagnosis.

Turn: Transcript turn 22 · Part 2: Process changes · Blocks: day-switch, notes, owners, effect · Theme: Plan paper · Review: Approved 1 Oct with the Bed Management Solutions turns.

Desktop canvas · 864px
Part 2 · Process changes

Run the two jobs together

Today one team discharges, then admits. The change is to run both at once, against beds that will be free.

Part 2 of 5Process changes
  1. Idea
  2. Shaped
  3. Tested with you
  4. Agreed

One team. Discharges first, then admissions. Patients reach a bed between 4:30 and 8 PM.Both jobs run together, against beds that will be free. The goal is a bed by about noon.

8 AM10 AMnoon2 PM4 PM6 PM8 PM

Admissions
Admissions afterAdmissions alongside

4:30 to 8 PMBy about noon

Your own times: patients arrive at about 1 PM and reach a bed between 4:30 and 8 PM. The noon time is a goal.

  1. Change 1

    Give beds forward

    Today a bed is given only once it is confirmed ready. Give it against when it will be free instead. The same people and beds then make a different day.

Pick a route to follow it through the maze.

  2. Ruled out

    Fix what gets decided

    A rule on who goes home would sit on top of a clinical call. Doctors would break it daily, and they would be right to.

    Why it fails
    Clinical calls cannot be timetabled
  4. Ruled out

    No fixed times at all

    Without fixed times, nobody can plan the evening before. That is how the day runs now: rebuilt every afternoon.

    Why it fails
    Nothing is ready the evening before
  6. The way through

    Fix when decisions are made

    The times are fixed. The decisions are not. A step-down that slips is an input to the next pass, not a breach.

    When the 2 PM, 5 PM and 6 PM decisions happen
    Left alone
    Who is fit to leave, emergencies, a step-down that slips

The six teams, and what each one receives
  1. Doctors

    Speak on the round

    None beyond the round

    What changes
    The time, not the job

    Told when to call

    What changes
    Fewer calls, made at the right time

    In your message
  4. Discharge team

    A release deadline per bed

    The discharge team gets a deadline for each bed it is releasing, instead of a surprise in the afternoon.

    What changes
    A deadline they can plan to
    Who leads your discharge team today?
    In your message
  5. Billing

    One new report

    Bill close and bill open, read against the same bed. Both facts already exist in your system.

    What changes
    One report, run weekly
    Who runs billing reports today?
    In your message
  6. IT

    Read access, once

    Your IT team gives read access to the systems you already run. After that, nothing more is asked.

    What changes
    One piece of work at the start
    Who in IT would we work with?
    In your message

Medical Supervisory

One round at 5 PM

One fixed round, only for beds expected to free tomorrow. They confirm or correct by 5 PM, so the plan freezes at 6 PM.

What changes
The time, not the job
Who leads Medical Supervisory today?
In your message
Admissions desk

Told when to call

The desk stops guessing. It is told when to call each patient in, bed by bed.

What changes
Fewer calls, made at the right time
Who runs your admissions desk today?
In your message
Discharge team

A release deadline per bed

The discharge team gets a deadline for each bed it is releasing, instead of a surprise in the afternoon.

What changes
A deadline they can plan to
Who leads your discharge team today?
In your message
Billing

One new report

Bill close and bill open, read against the same bed. Both facts already exist in your system.

What changes
One report, run weekly
Who runs billing reports today?
In your message
IT

Read access, once

Your IT team gives read access to the systems you already run. After that, nothing more is asked.

What changes
One piece of work at the start
Who in IT would we work with?
In your message
Where the resistance sits
A date a day early

Naming a discharge date a day ahead is a clinical call. Checking a predicted date is not.

Extra clinical time
None beyond the round

This claim is wrong if the round gets longer to give the date. We would measure that from the first week.

Bed Management Solutions drawings

One main drawing per turn, so no two turns look alike. Drawn by bm_so_blocks.py and bm_so_blocks2.py beside the generator. Each says which library motif it is built from.

heading Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

Built from: library heading. Eyebrow, title and deck, with the door plate from the Solutions landing page: which part this is and where it stands (idea, shaped, tested with you, agreed).

Use when: every turn
Avoid when: never twice
Drawn in: bm-so-01, shown above

circuit Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library motif: the lightbulb; the chain wrapped three and three with an elbow. The steps of one part as switches on one wire, from where the data starts to a bulb that lights only when every switch is on.

Use when: a part that is a sequence of steps, each needing the one before; showing that the outcome only arrives at the end of the chain
Avoid when: parts that do not depend on each other
Interaction: Pick a switch: it is raised and its sheet opens, the current runs from the plug to it, and the bulb lights at the last switch.
Drawn in: bm-so-01, shown above

jigsaw Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library motif: the jigsaw (puzzle piece geometry from solutions_html.py). The steps of one part as jigsaw pieces locked together. Picking a piece lifts it and outlines the pieces it relies on.

Use when: showing that the steps only work together; one step makes another worth anything
Avoid when: the overview of the five parts (use the library puzzle)
Interaction: Pick a piece: it lifts, the pieces it relies on are outlined, and its sheet opens. On a phone the sheet opens under the piece.
Drawn in: bm-so-01, shown above

route Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

Built from: library route (Solutions), layered. The library route: stations on a trail, each opening its sheet, then a fork under the bulb with doors to what comes next.

Use when: steps in order that end in a choice of where to go next
Avoid when: no choice at the end
Interaction: Pick a station to raise it and open its sheet. A door writes its line into the chat message.
Drawn in: bm-so-01, shown above

effect Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: 07 §5.2 effect box. The quantity the part is aimed at, named once. Its look changes from turn to turn: door plate, stamp, ticket, banner, meter.

Use when: the part has one number it moves
Avoid when: more than two in a turn
Drawn in: bm-so-01, shown above

hub Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library motif: the lightbulb; the converge pattern with a rail. What the hospital provides, wired into one engine, and what comes out of it.

Use when: how a part is achieved; showing that many steps are one build
Avoid when: a sequence in time
Interaction: Pick an input: its wire lights and the outputs it feeds light up. Its sheet opens.
Drawn in: bm-so-02, shown above

pair Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: 07 §5.2, two effect boxes side by side. Two boxes read against each other: a prerequisite and a blocker, worth and cost, a claim and what would prove it wrong.

Use when: two facts that belong together
Avoid when: more than two
Interaction: Each box can carry an Ask button that writes its line into the message.
Drawn in: bm-so-02, shown above

foundation Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library motif: the drafting sheet; a building section. What Tojo brings above the ground line, what must already be there below it, and a switch for a hospital still on paper.

Use when: what we supply against what must exist
Avoid when: no threshold to state
Interaction: Pick a box to open it. The switch redraws the building for a hospital that is mostly on paper.
Drawn in: bm-so-03, shown above

doors Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the Solutions landing page: the corridor of fixes and its door plates. The five parts as doors off one corridor. A covered part stands ajar. Each closed door carries the question its part answers.

Use when: progress through the parts; what is left to cover
Avoid when: the first reveal
Interaction: Pick a door to open its sheet and go into that part.
Drawn in: bm-so-04, shown above

day-switch Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library untangle: the Today / With switch on real times. The day as it runs now against the day as it would run, lane by lane on one clock.

Use when: a process change shown on the real day
Avoid when: no times to show
Interaction: Switch between the two days. Bars move to their new times.
Drawn in: bm-so-05, shown above

notes Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library drafting sheets, pinned. A few pinned drafting cards, each opening its sheet.

Use when: a handful of smaller items beside a main drawing
Avoid when: the main drawing of a turn
Interaction: Pick a card to raise it and open its sheet.
Drawn in: bm-so-05, shown above

owners Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: 07 visual grammar: amber for new roles, a two-way arrow for peers. Two owners as peers, joined by a two-way arrow, with the one line that explains why both are needed.

Use when: two roles that only work together
Avoid when: one role
Interaction: Pick an owner to open what the job is.
Drawn in: bm-so-05, shown above

maze Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library maze (Solutions), layered. The library maze: routes ruled out and the way through, now with the layer.

Use when: a challenge: why not just do something else?
Avoid when: no routes to rule out
Interaction: Pick a route: its trail walks the maze and its sheet opens. The way through lights the bulb.
Drawn in: bm-so-06, shown above

rerun Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library route, drawn as a loop. Try a change: the plan re-runs, new call-in times go out, and the change is recorded.

Use when: showing that a change is handled, not a rule broken
Avoid when: nothing re-runs
Interaction: Pick a change. The loop runs again, box by box, and its sheet says what moved.
Drawn in: bm-so-06, shown above

gap-knots Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library knots: the rope and its knots, undone. A chain whose waiting sits in the gaps between steps, drawn as knots. Switch to an owner and the knots come undone.

Use when: nobody owns the gaps
Avoid when: the wait is inside a step
Interaction: Pick a gap to see who waits there. Switch to see the chain with an owner.
Drawn in: bm-so-07, shown above

people Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the Bed Management home page: rooms on a ward plan; 07 sign-off tag. Six teams as rooms on one plan, each with what it receives, then who signs it off and the two managers under them.

Use when: key people and buy-in
Avoid when: headcount
Interaction: Pick a room to see what changes for that team.
Drawn in: bm-so-08, shown above

sizing Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library chain pattern, with a live slider. The roles, then the two sizing chains: one settled, one waiting on the hospital’s figures.

Use when: teams and numbers
Avoid when: no sizing
Interaction: Pick a role to open it. Move the slider and the headcount changes. Type a figure into the chain that waits for it.
Drawn in: bm-so-09, shown above

costing Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: 07 §5 effect and fill-in fields. What can be costed now, and the numbers still needed, typed in place.

Use when: a cost with gaps
Avoid when: no gaps
Interaction: Type each missing number in place. Every entry goes into the message.
Drawn in: bm-so-09, shown above

gauges Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: library motif: the drafting instrument; the landing page stops. The measures as dials. New ones are dashed with no needle, because nobody reads them today.

Use when: what to measure
Avoid when: fewer than four measures
Interaction: Pick a dial to open it. Filter to the early warnings or the results.
Drawn in: bm-so-10, shown above

findings Bed Management Solutions drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: 07: muted fill for the hospital’s own facts. The hospital’s own findings, muted, because they are its facts and not our proposals.

Use when: a summary
Avoid when: new findings
Interaction: Pick a finding to open where it came from.
Drawn in: bm-so-11, shown above

the three buttons every turn
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

On every turn, not only landing pages (rules/08 §8): Proceed with next step (naming the step), Add more, Jump to the next place. Same order and look as the landing page. The generator refuses a spec without canvas.actions.

Automations turn templates

Each is drawn by Bed Management/automations-html-generator/bm_automations_html.py from its spec, with the Automations motifs of this library (the switchboard, the engine on a screen, the station panel, the desk helper, the relay, the thinker, the night shift) in Bed Management’s Automations colours (the station panel), with the common tool layer. Every turn ends with the three buttons: Proceed with next step, Add more, Jump to Processes.

heading Bed Management Automations drawing
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

Avoid when: never twice

sources Bed Management Automations drawing
approvedUniversal pattern · drawn here for Bed Management

Built from: library sources (Automations), layered, with the landing page’s main switch. The records as switches, the main switch every automation waits on, and the automations as lamps that light only when every record they need is linked.

Use when: how an automation is built; what has to be linked first
Avoid when: nothing to link
Interaction: Flip a switch to link a record. Pick a record to open what your IT team gives. Lamps light when all their records are on.

brain Bed Management Automations drawing

Use when: what the engine reads and makes, over a day
Avoid when: no flow of records
Interaction: Pick a time of day or play the day. The records light as they arrive and the answers fill.

panel Bed Management Automations drawing
approvedBed Management only

Avoid when: a single automation
Interaction: Step through the phases; lamps light to each row’s stage. Pick a row to open it.

Avoid when: nothing asked of IT

Processes turn templates

11 turns in conversation order, drawn by Bed Management/processes-html-generator/bm_processes_html.py from their specs: the Processes motifs of this library (the ward board, the magnets, the name badges, the chairs and lamps, the instrument windows, the loop, the trial strip) and five Bed Management drawings (the day on a wall clock, the trial ward with pins, the doctor’s round cards, the OPD slip, the clipboard), in the trial ward look: pale clay, deep brown, rust. Every turn ends with the three buttons: Proceed with next step, Add more, Jump to Diagnosis.

    Admissions start after 1 PM

    Check a date, by voice

    None, the round already happens

    In bed by about noon

One rule keeps the day late

0 of 5 moved
Step, and whoTodayWith the change
  1. Admissions desk

    Bed given out

    This one rule causes the late afternoon. A bed is only given once it is ready, so every step after it waits.

    Today
    Given when ready
    New
    Given against its free time
    Who decides a bed is ready today?
    In your message
  2. Admissions desk

    Patient called in

    Today every patient is told the same time. With a free time for each bed, each patient gets their own.

    Today
    One time for all
    New
    One time per bed
    What time are patients told to come today?
    In your message
  3. Admissions desk

    Admission papers

    Papers take about an hour of your 3½ hours. Done while the bed is still being cleaned, they stop adding to the wait.

    Paperwork today
    About 1 hour of 3½
    New
    Done while the bed is cleaned
    Which paper takes longest at your desk?
    In your message
  4. Housekeeping

    Bed cleaned

    Housekeeping hears the leaving time from the plan. They are at the bed when it empties.

    Today
    Called when someone notices
    New
    Told from the plan
    How does housekeeping hear a bed is empty?
    In your message
  5. Billing

    First bill on bed

    The bed earns again only when the new bill opens. Bringing it to noon is the money in this whole change.

    Today
    From 5 PM, up to 8 PM
    Goal
    By about noon
    When does the first charge go on today?
    In your message

Processes · a date not given

No date is not a breakdown

What happens to one bed when the doctor does not confirm. Step round it.

Ward boardA date not given
  1. Changes
  2. People
  3. Roles
  4. Measures
  5. The trial

Step round the loop, or pick a step. At the check, the answer sends you on or back.

Round 1Every day, before 6 PM
  2. Step 1 of 5

    No date given

    The doctor is busy or unsure. Nothing breaks. The patient simply has no confirmed date yet.

    Happens
    Often, at the start
    Which teams would confirm least at first?
    In your message
  4. Step 2 of 5

    Likely date used

    Tojo uses the usual stay for this kind of patient. The bed is planned as likely, not confirmed.

    Marked
    Likely, not confirmed
    Do you track usual stays by procedure?
    In your message
  6. Step 3 of 5

    Checked at 5 PM

    The 5 PM round asks the doctor once more. Most dates are settled here, before the freeze.

    Did the doctor confirm by 5 PM?
    By
    5 PM, every day
    Who would ask the doctor at 5 PM?
    In your message
  8. Step 4 of 5

    Planned as confirmed

    The bed goes into the 6 PM plan with a call-in time for the next patient.

    Gives
    A call-in time
    Who sends call-in times today?
    In your message
  10. Step 5 of 5

    Likely, asked again

    The bed stays in the plan as likely. No patient is called in for it until the doctor confirms next morning.

    Patient called
    Only once confirmed
    How often would a likely bed be wrong?
    In your message

    What the doctor decides

The bed plan starts in OPD

  1. Changes
  2. People
  3. Roles
  4. Measures

OPD prescription · OrthopaedicsAn example slip, written in OPD on Tuesday
Rx
  2. Line 1

    Procedure

    The procedure tells the plan which ward and which kind of bed.

    Feeds
    Ward and bed type

    Admit on

    Today
    Found on the day
    New
    Held days ahead

  6. Line 3

    Likely stay

    Feeds
    The next free time
    Do OPD doctors write a likely stay today?
    In your message
  8. Line 4

    Operation theatre

    A theatre slot booked with the bed, so the stay does not start with a wait.

    Feeds
    The theatre list
    Who books theatre slots today?
    In your message
  10. Line 5

    ICU after?

    If an ICU bed is needed after the procedure, it is planned with the ward bed.

    Feeds
    The ICU plan
    How often do planned patients need ICU?
    In your message
  12. Line 6

    Paid by

    Insurance approval can start before the patient arrives, not on the day.

    Feeds
    The insurance desk
    How long do approvals take here?
    In your message

Bed Management Processes drawings

The five new drawings live in bm_pr_blocks.py; the library Processes motifs are loaded from Discharge Process/processes-html-generator/dp_pr_blocks.py as a private copy and drawn in the trial ward colours.

swap Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Each step of the day, its magnet moved from today to with the changes.

Use when: what changes on the ward, step by step
Avoid when: fewer than three steps
Interaction: Pick a step to open it. Move one magnet, or all of them with the switch.
Drawn in: bm-pr-03, shown above

trial Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The two weeks on one ward: the day strip you can play, the phases as pickable bands, the ward still to choose.

Use when: scoping a short trial
Avoid when: no trial
Interaction: Pick a phase, or play the two weeks. Type the ward you choose.
Drawn in: bm-pr-10, shown above

badges Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Name badges on the board, grouped by what each person does: who agrees, who is still to ask, who has a worry.

Use when: who has to agree, team by team
Avoid when: one approver only
Interaction: Pick a badge to open it. Filter by the trial or still to ask.
Drawn in: bm-pr-07, shown above

seats Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The roles as chairs, their triggers as lamps, the busy-hours check as a day strip with a slider.

Use when: whether to hire, and how many
Avoid when: no new roles
Interaction: Pick a role to open it. Move the slider and switch the sizing rule.
Drawn in: bm-pr-08, shown above

readouts Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. The measures as instrument windows: the starting number where there is one, dashed where nobody has one yet.

Use when: the measures to watch
Avoid when: fewer than three measures
Interaction: Pick a window to open it. Filter by when it is read; flip to after the trial.
Drawn in: bm-pr-09, shown above

loop Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. Plan, try, measure, adjust, spread: a wheel with a yes-or-no check that sends you on or back.

Use when: what happens after a trial
Avoid when: a one-off step
Interaction: Step round, or pick a step. At the check, answer yes or not yet.
Drawn in: bm-pr-05, shown above

timesheet Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: the library Processes motifs (processes_html.py), layered. One normal day’s times on one line. Blank: the times are typed straight into the drawing. Filled: the times and the gaps between them.

Use when: asking for real times; showing them back
Avoid when: no times
Interaction: Type a time on each step (blank), or pick a step to open it (filled).
Drawn in: not used yet, shown above

day-dial Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: new (bm_pr_blocks.py): a wall clock, 8 AM to 8 PM, with the library Processes switch (today or with the changes). The ward's day on a clock: today's admission window against the new one, and the fixed times of the new day.

Use when: how the day changes on the wards
Avoid when: more than 8 fixed times
Interaction: Switch between today and the new day. Pick a time to move the clock hand and open it.
Drawn in: bm-pr-01, shown above

ward-pins Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: new (bm_pr_blocks.py): the trial ward seen from above, from the approved Processes landing page B. Each change pinned in the room of the ward where it happens.

Use when: where on the ward each change happens
Avoid when: more than 7 changes
Interaction: Pick a change to raise its pin on the ward plan and open it.
Drawn in: bm-pr-02, shown above

round-cards Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: new (bm_pr_blocks.py): the doctor's round as patient cards, after the transcript's 'show a date to confirm or correct'. A card per patient with the predicted date the doctor confirms or changes on the round.

Use when: what a doctor does on the round
Avoid when: more than 6 patients
Interaction: Pick a patient to open where the date comes from. Confirm the date, or change it and type the new one.
Drawn in: bm-pr-04, shown above

slip Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: new (bm_pr_blocks.py): the OPD prescription as a paper slip, its lines pulled into the bed plan. Where planned admissions come from: each line of the OPD slip and what it feeds in the bed plan.

Use when: the OPD slip as the start of the bed plan
Avoid when: more than 7 lines
Interaction: Pick a line to open it. Press the button to pull the slip into the bed plan.
Drawn in: bm-pr-06, shown above

clipboard Bed Management Processes drawing
approvedBed Management only

Built from: new (bm_pr_blocks.py): a clipboard form, typed straight into the drawing (the tool layer's inline entries). What we need from the hospital to start, each line typed in and added to the message.

Use when: asking for the numbers or names still missing
Avoid when: more than 7 lines
Interaction: Type on each line. Every line typed is added to the chat message. Pick a line to see why it is needed.
Drawn in: bm-pr-11, shown above
